---
title: "Traits and Generics: Behaviour Without Inheritance"
description: "One key Rust idea, one tiny executable example, the reason it works, and a precise pitfall."
---

## The question

**How can one function print the name of different user-defined types?**

A trait defines required behaviour; a generic constraint says which types may be passed. It is a *capability contract*, not classical subclass inheritance.

## The core rule

`impl Trait` and `T: Trait` describe behaviour available on concrete types.

## One complete example

Paste these lines into `main.rs` and run with `rustc --edition 2024 main.rs && ./main`, or [use the tested Rust examples project](examples/index.qmd).

~~~rust
trait Named { fn name(&self) -> &str; }
struct User(&'static str);
impl Named for User {
    fn name(&self) -> &str { self.0 }
}
fn show<T: Named>(item: &T) { println!("{}", item.name()); }
fn main() { show(&User("Ada")); } // Ada
~~~

**Walk through it:** `Named` defines a method; `User` implements it; `show<T: Named>` accepts any type that implements the trait. `&self` borrows the receiver.

## Common misunderstanding

Rust's coherence/orphan rules limit where external traits may be implemented for external types. `dyn Named` is dynamic dispatch; `T: Named` typically uses static dispatch and monomorphisation.

## Remember it in one sentence

`impl Trait` and `T: Trait` describe behaviour available on concrete types.

**Official reference:** [The Rust Programming Language / Rust Reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch10-02-traits.html).
